title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time, the day and the month, make an appointment, and understand why the days of the week sound like numbers.
bekal: name the days, the months and the parts of the day
make a simple appointment with a time and a place

notes: **سَاعَة has two meanings at once: "hour/clock" and "o'clock".** كَمِ السَّاعَةُ؟ = "what time is it?", but نِصْفُ سَاعَةٍ = "half an hour (in length)". Context separates them, and in practice it is never confusing.

**Clock times use ordinal numbers, not ordinary ones.** Not "three o'clock" but "the third hour": اَلسَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ. All of them are feminine, because they agree with the feminine word سَاعَة. That's good news: you only need to learn one set of forms.
**إِلَّا means "to" (minus).** اَلرَّابِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا = "a quarter to four" = 3:45 p.m. Literally "the fourth except a quarter". For "past", use وَ: اَلرَّابِعَةُ وَالرُّبْعُ = 4:15 p.m.

**Most day names are numbers.** اَلْأَحَد (the first), اَلِاثْنَيْنِ (the second), اَلثُّلَاثَاء (the third), اَلْأَرْبِعَاء (the fourth), اَلْخَمِيس (the fifth). Only two are not numbers: اَلْجُمُعَة (the day of gathering, for Friday prayers) and اَلسَّبْت (the day of rest, related to *sabbath*).

**يَوْمَ الثُّلَاثَاءِ — "on Tuesday".** Notice that يَوْم takes a fatha with no preposition: this form expresses time. You can also use فِي: فِي يَوْمِ الثُّلَاثَاءِ. Both are correct; the first is shorter and more common.

**بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ literally "after midday".** Parts of the day are often named after the prayer times — not because every sentence is religious, but because that is how everyone divides the day: اَلْفَجْر, اَلظُّهْر, اَلْعَصْر, اَلْمَغْرِب, اَلْعِشَاء.
**فِي أَيِّ سَاعَةٍ؟ — the full "at what time?".** أَيّ means "which", and it is always followed by an indefinite noun with a kasra: أَيُّ كِتَابٍ؟ (which book?), فِي أَيِّ يَوْمٍ؟ (on which day?).

**لَا تَتَأَخَّرْ — a negative command.** "Don't ..." is لَا + the present-tense verb with a sukun at the end: لَا تَتَأَخَّرْ (don't be late), لَا تَنْسَ (don't forget), لَا تَقْلَقْ (don't worry). To a woman add ـِي: لَا تَتَأَخَّرِي.
**بِكُلِّ سُرُورٍ** literally "with all pleasure" — exactly "with pleasure". It's the standard polite answer to an invitation or a request for help.

grammars.title: Telling the time
after: Minutes are added with وَ (past) or إِلَّا (to): اَلثَّالِثَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ (3:30), اَلثَّالِثَةُ وَالرُّبْعُ (3:15), اَلثَّالِثَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا (2:45), اَلثَّالِثَةُ وَعِشْرُونَ دَقِيقَةً (3:20), اَلثَّالِثَةُ وَالثُّلْثُ (3:20, short version).
Morning or evening is added at the end: صَبَاحًا (a.m., morning), ظُهْرًا (midday), مَسَاءً (p.m., evening), لَيْلًا (at night). اَلسَّاعَةُ السَّابِعَةُ مَسَاءً = seven in the evening.

grammars.title: Days and months
after: So the Arab week counts its days: Sunday is "day one", Monday "day two", and so on up to Thursday, "day five". Once you know the numbers 1–5, you practically know the days already — just watch the vowels.

Western calendar months are borrowed too, but they differ by country: يَنَايِر (January) in Egypt and the Gulf, كَانُون الثَّانِي in Syria and Lebanon. The Islamic (Hijri) months are the same everywhere: مُحَرَّم, رَمَضَان, شَوَّال, ذُو الْحِجَّة.

sections.title: Parts of the day and time words

blocks.text: Notice that many time words end in tanween fatha: غَدًا, أَحْيَانًا, دَائِمًا, أَبَدًا, صَبَاحًا. That ـًا ending is the Arabic "adverb" marker — a bit like English *-ly* — just as in شُكْرًا ("thankfully, thanks") and أَهْلًا. Once you see the pattern, these words stop feeling random.

blocks.title: The weekend in the Arab world
items: In most Arab countries the weekend falls on **Friday and Saturday**, not Saturday–Sunday. In Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Jordan, Sunday is an ordinary working day.

This matters when you make plans: عُطْلَةُ نِهَايَةِ الْأُسْبُوعِ (*'uṭlatu nihaayatil-usbuu'* — the weekend) does not necessarily mean the same days as back home. A safe question: هَلْ أَنْتَ حُرٌّ يَوْمَ الْأَحَدِ؟ ("are you free on Sunday?").

blocks.text: One phrase is used constantly and mistranslated constantly: إِنْ شَاءَ اللهُ ("if God wills"). It is neither "maybe" nor a polite no — it is the standard way to talk about any future plan, used by Muslims and Christians alike. Accepting an invitation without it can even sound a little presumptuous to some speakers.

كَمِ السَّاعَةُ الْآنَ؟ — اَلسَّاعَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ. — مَتَى يَبْدَأُ الدَّرْسُ؟ — يَوْمَ الثُّلَاثَاءِ بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ. — أَنَا مَشْغُولٌ الْيَوْمَ. — إِلَى الْغَدِ!
اَلْأَحَد — اَلِاثْنَيْن — اَلثُّلَاثَاء — اَلْأَرْبِعَاء — اَلْخَمِيس — اَلْجُمُعَة — اَلسَّبْت

Example: اَلسَّاعَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ صَبَاحًا. — أَبْدَأُ عَمَلِي فِي السَّاعَةِ التَّاسِعَةِ. — لَا، أَنَا حُرٌّ غَدًا. — أَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ. — أَنَامُ فِي السَّاعَةِ الْعَاشِرَةِ.
wave: For the next three days, every time you look at a clock, say the time to yourself in Arabic. It's the cheapest drill there is.
